event.family_marine_01_before_dawn.choic: You clutch his sleeve. Your father stops in the middle of the motion.
You push his boots toward him. He realizes you saw the recall order.
You do not move. Your eyes follow every buckle, button, and movement.
event.family_marine_01_before_dawn.title: Before Dawn
event.family_marine_01_before_dawn.text: A recall order hits the door before dawn. Your father pulls his boots back on under the lamp. There is nobody else to stay with you when he leaves.
event.family_marine_01_before_dawn_i01_t: You tighten your grip. He has to gently pry your fingers loose before leaving.
You hand him what he forgot. He thanks you before stepping outside.
He meets your eyes, then looks down at the order as if he owes an explanation.
Your father pauses at the threshold, the folded order in one hand. Outside, the Marine waiting for him avoids looking in.
event.family_marine_01_before_dawn_i02_a: You refuse to forget that he left despite you.
You put away the rest of his things as if it were already your responsibility.
You remember the door, the lamp, and the sound of his boots.
The door closes. His footsteps fade before the room stops feeling too large.
event.family_marine_01_family_pennant.ch: You grab the blue cloth before the Marine finishes his sentence.
You immediately hand the pennant back to its owner.
Your finger traces the emblem's lines without leaving the cloth.
event.family_marine_01_family_pennant.te: A Marine from the neighborhood brings a small blue pennant for the household window. He sets it within reach while speaking with the adult beside you.
event.family_marine_01_family_pennant_i0: He laughs and says you already seem to recognize Marine colors.
He nods, surprised by your seriousness.
He names the emblem and shows you where it will be visible from the street.
The Marine crouches to take the pennant back, then pauses when he sees what you are doing.
The symbol quickly becomes something familiar in the household.
You watch the pennant as something that belongs to the adults first.
You memorize the emblem well enough to recognize it elsewhere.
The pennant is fixed to the window. Passing Marines recognize it at a glance; everyone else looks a little longer.
event.family_marine_01_no_box_on_form.ch: You stay put while he rearranges his equipment around you.
You push away the tool that keeps trying to force you into a measure that does not fit.
You watch the form while the clerk crosses out one box and searches for another.
You deliberately stretch your arm beyond the end of the ruler. The clerk calls someone else over.
event.family_marine_01_no_box_on_form.te: At the base family check, the clerk stops at a form designed for a Human child. Its chair, ruler, or boxes simply do not match your body.
event.family_marine_01_no_box_on_form_i0: Show what works
You show him where to place things so they stop getting in your way.
Keep the tool away
You refuse to let him use the old method again, even to save time.
Follow his new notes
You watch the words he invents to replace the crossed-out box.
Ask how far the string goes
The clerk unrolls the entire string. A quartermaster at the far desk turns around.
They Improvise
The clerk gives up on the standard setup. He fetches string, a second stool, and a blank sheet while the line waits behind you.
Look at the new entry
For once, the form changes around you.
Turn away from the desk
You leave after forcing the adults to respect a clear boundary.
Remember the correction
You mostly remember the moment the adult had to invent another way to do it.
Watch the quartermaster note your name
The quartermaster writes your name separately before handing the form back.
The Corrected Record
The clerk finally writes something that fits you instead of forcing the old box. The record goes back toward the base archives.
event.family_marine_04_empty_chair.choic: You push away the adult's hand when they try to take the chair.
You fold the chair yourself before the celebration ends.
Your voice breaks and several adults stare without knowing what to say.
They tell you a Marine cannot always choose. The chair stays empty.
The neighbor about to move the chair leaves it alone.
The small row around you agrees to keep the seat empty until the end.
event.family_marine_04_empty_chair.title: The Empty Chair
event.family_marine_04_empty_chair.text: Your father promised to be there for the neighborhood celebration. The benches fill, the second shift call sounds, and his chair stays empty.
event.family_marine_04_empty_chair_i01_w: You watch every uniform that passes at the end of the street.
You move the chair away so you no longer have to look at it.
Repeat it to anyone who asks
Every time someone asks, you give the same answer: he promised.
The celebration begins. Music covers the shift bell, but not the empty chair beside you.
event.family_marine_04_empty_chair_i02_t: You make him look at the ending celebration before accepting his excuse.
You are still angry, but you refuse to let his lateness erase the rest of the evening.
You head home before he can explain the mission.
Your father arrives as the benches are already emptying. He immediately sees the place you kept for him — or the one you put away.
You turn the box into a small job and stay near the wall.
You take the wrong passage and lose sight of the yellow line immediately.
You go too far before realizing you do not know how to get back.
You learn the rhythm of the corridors and move without being noticed.
You follow the base's movement while always keeping a route back to the storehouse.
The storekeeper gives you string and small tags to carry.
Nobody can watch you today. Your father settles you behind the base storehouse with a box of chalk and tells you not to cross the yellow line.
event.family_marine_04_you_come_to_base_: You become useful enough that the adults stop checking where you are every minute.
Keep going to the next corner
You push the exploration to where the corridors become unmistakably military.
People start recognizing you as “the storehouse kid” for the morning.
Boots keep crossing the yellow line. Every open door reveals a different piece of the base.
You follow the wrong coat and end up in a yard where nobody knows you.
A soldier brings you back to the storehouse before you find your father.
You spot the clearing passages and reach your father without obstructing the alert.
You anticipate the soldiers' movement and reach your father before he can come looking for you.
You stay exactly where you were left, even while everyone runs.
You push small crates and chalk out of the way so the adults can run.
A short siren sounds. Every adult suddenly changes direction, and the yellow line means little in the rush.
event.family_marine_04_dinner_interrupte: Pull him back to the table
You pull your father toward his chair. Your mother keeps her hand on the bowl.
Push his plate toward him
You push his plate toward his coat as if the choice were already made.
Say “Stay”
Your voice triggers the argument both adults were holding back.
Your father avoids your eyes and keeps hold of his coat.
Your father stops long enough for your mother to speak again.
Your father puts his coat back on the chair. Even the messenger waits for a different answer.
Dinner Interrupted
A Marine messenger knocks during dinner. Your father already reaches for his coat; your mother keeps a hand on his bowl and reminds him he promised to stay.
Stay beside your mother
Your father understands the cost of leaving before he even exits the room.
Hand him his coat
You hand him the coat. Your mother's silence grows heavier.
Ask who is right
The question forces them to explain what each had been demanding from the other.
Two Duties
Your father says the patrol is short-handed. Your mother answers that the household is too. The messenger remains at the threshold holding the order.
Accept that he goes
Your father leaves. Your mother stays beside you until his footsteps fade.
Ask him to stay tonight
Your father returns the order to the messenger and stays, at the cost of an explanation he will owe tomorrow.
Ask him to leave after dinner
The messenger agrees to wait a few minutes. For once, duty and family are not treated as an instant either-or choice.
The Messenger Waits
Nobody can pretend the decision is automatic: the messenger is still waiting, and dinner is getting cold.
event.family_marine_04_made_to_fit.choic: Show what gets in the way
You point out where the fabric pulls or blocks.
You test the fastenings one by one instead of making her guess.
You stand as still as you can while she works.
event.family_marine_04_made_to_fit.title: Made to Fit
event.family_marine_04_made_to_fit.text: A base seamstress opens the seams of a small practice jacket to adapt it to your body. She asks you to show her what gets in the way.
event.family_marine_04_made_to_fit_i01_f: You show her the exact movement that makes the jacket fail.
You suggest a different fastening instead of repeating the same setup.
You hold still a few more seconds before admitting it does not work.
The first version holds for a few seconds, then a seam pulls, a sleeve catches, or a fastening pops as soon as you move.
event.family_marine_04_made_to_fit_i02_f: The second version works because you helped shape it.
You move until you find the last weak spots, then she fixes them.
You let her apply what she just learned about your body.
The seamstress places the chalk in your hand and asks you to mark what she should change.
You take another piece of chalk and start a space beside theirs.
You force your way in and fall in front of everyone.
You step in, but the game stops around you.
You step in and refuse to leave. Eventually the game resumes.
You step in, move two markers, and show everyone another way to continue.
You stay outside the square and memorize their movements.
Children of Marines chalk out a drill square. When you approach, one blocks the entrance with a stick: “Not with this equipment.”
event.family_marine_04_off_drill_square_: Two children hesitate, then cross the chalk line toward you.
You stay there until someone agrees to resume the game.
From the edge, you copy a drill they just failed.
The other children turn toward you. The problem is no longer the equipment: they now have to decide what to do with your presence.
You describe the stick, the equipment, and the refusal. The adult has to answer something concrete.
You point to your own square instead of waiting for the adult to decide for you.
You give him no explanation. The group resumes, but the scene remains entirely between the children.
A Marine stops in front of the two chalk squares. He asks why the group is split before the other children can invent an excuse.
event.family_marine_04_quartermaster_mea: Stretch out both arms
You deliberately hold the pose and let him record everything.
Ask why
The officer cuts off your question and keeps measuring as if your opinion does not belong in the notebook.
He only says a Giant is “worth tracking.”
He admits some officers track Giant growth for military potential.
You keep asking until he explains what he records, for whom, and why your name matters.
Pull your arm back
You pull your arm back before the final measurement.
The Quartermaster's Measure
A quartermaster unrolls his measuring rope to the end, checks your reach, then writes your name in a notebook. At four, he already wants to know how large you will grow.
Look at the other entries
You realize this tracking existed before you and will continue after today.
Close the notebook
You place your hand on the page. The officer has to stop for the first time.
Point at your name
You make it clear you want to know why your name is there.
The Notebook
When the officer turns the page, you see other large measurements, ages, and notes about expected strength. Your name is not alone.
Accept testing, not deciding
You accept being tested, but not having your future decided for you.
Ask who decides for you
You refuse to let the notebook answer for you.
Refuse the tracking
You ask that your name not be used to prepare a career you never chose.
“Worth Tracking”
The officer finally says it plainly: some superiors want to identify Giants early who might one day serve in Marine forces.
Answer before your father
You answer for yourself. The officer writes that down too.
Let your father answer
You watch your father decide what he allows on your behalf.
Refuse yourself
You refuse clearly. Military tracking may continue elsewhere, but not with your consent.
In Front of Your Father
The officer finally asks your father whether he agrees to bring you back. This time, the question is asked in front of you.
event.family_marine_04_behind_office_doo: Press your ear to the door
The handle turns while your ear is still against the wood.
You catch a few words, then footsteps approach.
You understand the order concerns civilians your father believes would be endangered.
You hear the order, the refusal, and each man's reason before anyone approaches.
Call your father
You call him before hearing more. The argument stops behind the door.
Back away quietly
Your heel knocks over a bucket in the corridor.
You leave too late: your father spots you at the end of the corridor.
You leave the corridor unseen.
You leave silently and even memorize the route back.
Behind the Office Door
You wait in a base corridor. Behind the door, your father flatly refuses a patrol order. His superior reminds him that a Marine does not choose his missions.
Stay to the end
You stay long enough to understand the dispute is about specific people, not your father's pride.
Call him again
Your father finally opens the door. His superior immediately sees you were right outside.
Keep walking
You walk away knowing he said no, but not fully knowing why.
A Few Words Too Many
The word “civilians” carries through the door, then “risk.” Your father answers that an order can be lawful and still be wrong.
Ask him why
You ask him directly why he refused.
Pretend you heard nothing
You give him the chance to keep the argument to himself.
Say he was right
You take his side before he has fully explained himself.
The Door Opens
A few minutes later, your father finds you. He knows you were close enough to understand that he defied a superior.
Believe him
You discover that an uniform can contain refusal.
Ask what he risked
You understand his refusal could cost him something real.
Keep your doubt
You mainly remember that the same mission can have two different versions.
Why Did You Say No?
Your father finally chooses what to tell you: the order, the danger he saw, and what a Marine is supposed to do when the two no longer align.
event.family_marine_04_fallback_home.cho: You pull down the coat before it is soaked.
You deal with the overflow first.
You push the water back toward the door with whatever you can find.
event.family_marine_04_fallback_home.tex: Rain slips under the threshold while your father's service coat is already catching drops. The basin overflows and nobody tells you what to save first.
event.family_marine_04_fallback_home_i01: The coat is dry, but some floorboards are soaked.
You limited the damage by handling the most urgent source first.
Your arms tire before the rain does, but you kept the household afloat.
When the rain eases, the result of your first choice is obvious in the room.
You invent a difference and choose with far too much confidence.
You hesitate until the Marine takes both tokens back.
You spot a familiar scratch on the right token.
You spot the scratch and a wear mark the Marine had missed.
You immediately choose the wrong token.
You guess wrong and the Marine corrects you before the token leaves the counter.
You guess right without being able to explain why.
You guess right and the Marine laughs at your confidence.
You refuse to choose without proof.
At pay distribution, a Marine places two nearly identical tokens on the counter: one belongs to your household, the other to an absent family. He asks which one to take.
event.family_marine_04_fallback_service_: You leave with the right token and a better idea of how the base keeps its accounts.
You accept the written check over your intuition.
You memorize the detail that will let you rely less on someone else next time.
The Marine finally opens the pay ledger. Small notes beside the numbers explain why the two tokens look alike.
event.family_marine_04_fallback_adaptati: You gather what is nearby to make a place that fits you.
You let the adults move what is needed.
You refuse to be carried and stay standing beside the table.
In the base mess, the table reserved for families does not fit your body. An adult offers to carry you or move everyone else for you.
Nobody had to give up their place, and you did not need to be carried.
The adaptation becomes a shared task instead of a spectacle.
You keep your decision to the end despite the stares.
Benches scrape, trays shift, and every eye turns toward the solution you chose.
You refuse to leave the doorway until you hear his footsteps.
You go looking for someone who has to give you an answer.
You tidy up, heat water, and prepare whatever might help if he returns hurt.
event.family_marine_07_no_return.title: He Doesn't Come Home
event.family_marine_07_no_return.text: Your father's patrol was due back before nightfall. Two hours after the bell, his spare coat still hangs untouched and nobody comes to explain the delay.
event.family_marine_07_no_return_i01_rum: Your imagination immediately fills in everything the neighbor does not know.
You force the neighbor to admit he is repeating something heard at the port.
You refuse to let the household panic over a story with no names and no proof.
A neighbor says one patrol boat was damaged. He does not know which one or who was aboard.
event.family_marine_07_no_return_i02_at_: The guard sends you home and tells your father you tried to push past him verbally.
The guard repeats the rule without adding a word.
He at least confirms your father is alive and the patrol is returning on foot.
He gives you an estimated return time and confirms your father is escorting an injured Marine.
You sit outside the restricted area and turn waiting into a silent protest.
You leave without a full answer, but with something concrete to do.
At the base, the guard has no orders to give you information. Behind him, empty stretchers have still been prepared.
event.family_marine_07_no_return_i03_ret: You do not blame the mission; you blame him for leaving you without knowing.
You put your fear aside until the injured Marine is settled and your father can finally speak.
You refuse reassuring phrases and make him recount the facts in order.
Your father finally returns, covered in salt and mud, another Marine's arm over his shoulders. He is not injured, but he immediately sees what his delay did to you.
event.family_marine_07_sealed_packet.cho: You put both hands on it and ask who sent it.
You damage the edge of the seal by handling it too closely.
You recognize nothing useful on the seal.
You recognize the same symbol used in the storehouse ledger.
You also notice the Marine who came for it belongs to a different service.
You hand the packet to the uniformed adult without asking anything.
event.family_marine_07_sealed_packet.tex: A petty officer leaves a sealed packet on the counter and asks you to guard it for five minutes while he fetches your father. Another Marine coat arrives almost immediately to collect it.
event.family_marine_07_sealed_packet_i01: You keep the packet out of reach until he proves something.
You ask for the same kind of proof adults demand from one another.
You finally hand it over because the uniform feels like enough proof.
The Marine asking for the packet does not know the name of the petty officer who gave it to you. He grows impatient when you ask.
event.family_marine_07_sealed_packet_i02: You muddle the details and sound as if you invented your reasons afterward.
You explain poorly, but the petty officer understands you hesitated for a reason.
You clearly reconstruct who asked for what and in what order.
You even identify the service difference that first made you suspicious.
You admit you treated the uniform itself as proof.
You maintain that guarding the packet was your job until proven otherwise.
The petty officer comes running back and stops when he sees the packet — or its absence — between you.
event.family_marine_07_sealed_packet_i03: You remember that an order does not erase the need to verify who it belongs to.
You mainly remember that adults will eventually correct their own mistakes.
You turn the hesitation or wrong handoff into a personal rule for next time.
The packet finally reaches the right hands. The petty officer lets you see the receipt before leaving, as if he wants you to know how trust is verified.
event.family_marine_07_fathers_name.choi: You let the praise land on you as if it already belonged to you.
Say you have done nothing yet
You point out that the name has not passed the exercise for you.
You promise so much that the other children burst out laughing.
Your confidence sounds borrowed rather than convincing.
You turn the praise into a challenge to the group.
Even the officer laughs and asks you to prove that confidence during the exercise.
event.family_marine_07_fathers_name.text: An officer praises you in front of other children before the exercise even starts: “With your father's name, we already know what to expect.”
event.family_marine_07_fathers_name_i01_: You refuse to defend merit you have not earned yet.
You suggest the exercise decide what the name cannot prove.
You openly accept that your family's history already gives you something.
Another child says loudly enough to be heard: “They're praising his father. He hasn't done anything.”
event.family_marine_07_fathers_name_i02_: You miss the simplest move exactly when everyone is watching.
You finish without distinction and without disaster.
You do well enough that the others finally talk about what you did.
You perform clearly well, and your father's name stops being the only thing the officer talks about.
You do only what is required, refusing to turn the drill into a performance.
Help the child who challenged you
You choose to help them with their drill instead of defending your name.
The drill starts with every eye on you. Every move now seems expected to confirm or deny a story that existed before you.
event.family_marine_07_fathers_name_i03_: You clearly separate what your father did from what you just did.
Say you will carry the name
You accept the name as an expectation, but decide to turn it into a responsibility.
You refuse to let your father's past become a verdict on your future.
After the drill, the officer starts talking about your father again. This time, you have something of your own to place beside that name.
You stay on the uniformed side while the vendor empties the stall.
Help the vendor save their goods
You start moving what can still be saved before anyone stops you.
Your question lands like an accusation and your father cuts you off in front of everyone.
You are only told that rules are rules.
Your father admits the punishment is broader than the offense.
You force the responsible officer to explain publicly why no middle option exists.
event.family_marine_07_bad_order.title: The Bad Order
event.family_marine_07_bad_order.text: A patrol shuts down a local vendor's stall for a minor violation. Your father enforces the order while the vendor protests that all the goods will spoil by tomorrow.
event.family_marine_07_bad_order_i01_rul: Read the notice with your father
You verify he did not invent the rule: it really exists.
You separate what can be carried away from what will be lost.
You look for a way to enforce the order without destroying everything on the stall.
The order is valid, signed, and simple. The problem is what it concretely does to the vendor when enforced without flexibility.
event.family_marine_07_bad_order_i02_per: Say that is the price of the rule
You accept that enforcing the rule carries that cost.
You do whatever the order does not explicitly forbid to reduce the damage.
Ask your father if it is fair
You refuse to ask only whether it is legal.
The vendor places a damaged crate at your feet: even if the order is lifted tomorrow, this part will not come back.
event.family_marine_07_bad_order_i03_fat: You decide the consistency of the rule matters more than what it cost today.
You keep the distinction between obeying correctly and doing something just.
Ask what he would do without the uniform
You force him to separate his personal judgment from the role he just carried out.
When the stall is empty, your father no longer has the rule in front of him. He now has to answer as your father, not only as a Marine.
event.family_marine_07_not_on_list.choic: The organizer bristles and says he cannot rewrite the list for one person.
He promises to think about it next time, which solves nothing today.
He agrees to make a temporary place for you today.
He changes the list in front of you and asks what equipment is actually needed.
You suggest a version your body can actually take part in.
You refuse to stand around waiting for a box to appear for you.
event.family_marine_07_not_on_list.title: Not on the List
event.family_marine_07_not_on_list.text: At an activity reserved for Marine families, the organizer looks for your name and stops: the column for your equipment or body type is blank.
event.family_marine_07_not_on_list_i01_p: You refuse to let the decision be made away from you.
You take the equipment and show exactly what needs to change.
You leave before the adults turn your absence into a minor logistical detail.
The other families wait while the organizer decides: include you, improvise something, or continue without you.
event.family_marine_07_not_on_list_i02_o: Invite them to try your version
A few try your adaptation and discover it works for them too.
Ask only for your own place
You refuse to prove the solution benefits everyone just to deserve a place.
The activity resumes, but your absence becomes visible instead of disappearing into an empty box.
The other children realize the decision made about you may change the activity for them too.
event.family_marine_07_not_on_list_i03_r: Make sure he changes the list
Your name and a concrete solution remain on the sheet after you leave.
You leave mainly knowing you can make your own place without waiting for perfect permission.
You do not forget how easily the organization continued without you.
At the end, the organizer keeps the sheet. He has to decide what he will write for next time.
event.family_marine_07_old_sergeant.choi: The sergeant smiles as if he knows exactly which version you expect.
You ask him to leave out plaques, ranks, and polished words.
Say you do not want to hear it
The sergeant stops, but makes it clear he will keep the story if you change your mind.
event.family_marine_07_old_sergeant.text: An old sergeant recognizes your name during a base formality. He says he served with your father and asks whether anyone ever told you “the broken bridge story.”
event.family_marine_07_old_sergeant_i01_: You ask about the brave act before the mistake.
You focus on the mistake official stories could easily omit.
You refuse to choose which half of the story matters.
The sergeant says your father saved two comrades from a collapsed bridge — after ignoring an order that would have kept them away from it.
event.family_marine_07_old_sergeant_i02_: Remember he went back for the others
You decide that making things right matters even when the mistake comes first.
You refuse to let the rescue erase the source of the danger.
You refuse to turn your father into either a pure hero or a pure fool.
The sergeant removes nothing: your father disobeyed out of pride, then risked his life to repair what his choice caused.
event.family_marine_07_old_sergeant_i03_: You choose to keep the courage without forgetting it came after a mistake.
You prefer a memory that resists polished stories.
Refuse to make it your story
You accept his past exists without deciding it must become your model.
The sergeant lets you leave with the one version he promises not to simplify if you ever ask again.
event.family_marine_07_giant_demonstrati: Do the planned test
You accept the announced program, no more and no less.
Choose the safest exercise
You choose the task least likely to turn your strength into a spectacle.
Ask what the test proves
They answer that the demonstration does not need your opinion to be useful.
The officer vaguely says they need numbers.
He admits they are already comparing your progress to other military profiles.
He explains exactly which performances would trigger closer monitoring.
The Demonstration
The officers have prepared weights, ropes, and targets to “see where you are.” This time, they ask in front of several adults what you are actually willing to demonstrate.
Lift cleanly
The load tips and slips from your grip.
You move forward, but the load drifts toward the edge of the lane.
You control the load and still have room to spare.
You finish with enough control that the officers stop talking only about raw strength.
Take more time
You refuse to turn the test into a race and keep the load under control.
Ask for a spotter
You demand a safety measure nobody had planned for the visitors.
The Test Begins
The first task looks simple: move a load to a mark without leaving the lane painted on the ground.
Finish your move first
You finish the exercise before turning toward the accident.
Drop the test and protect the helper
You immediately abandon the performance to block the crate's path.
Shout for them to move
You use your voice before your strength to get the helper out of danger.
The Rope Gives
A restraint rope snaps behind you. A small equipment crate starts sliding toward a young helper standing too close to the area.
Defend your choice
You lose your temper and the officer reduces the discussion to your attitude.
He insists the test should have been completed even though nobody was hurt.
You make him admit that a Marine who ignores someone in danger has failed something more important than a timer.
Even the other officers repeat your argument before the supervisor can close the discussion.
Accept their scoring
You let the adults decide the measurable performance was the only important part.
Ask if the helper is okay first
You refuse to discuss the score before checking the person who was endangered.
What Actually Counts
The accident is over. The responsible officer looks first at the timer, then at the helper, then at you.
Make them record the protective choice
The note in your file mentions protection before performance.
Make them record the best result
You choose to make the file remember first what your body can do.
Make them record your safety conditions
You make them record that the next demonstration cannot be organized as if nobody else exists around it.
What They Write Down
The officers fill out the same kind of notebook as four years earlier. This time, you can see whether the line records only strength or judgment too.
event.family_marine_07_not_an_exhibit.ch: You leave before he finishes the introduction.
Say no in front of them
Your anger lets the officer present your refusal as a tantrum.
He smiles and tries to continue despite your refusal.
The visitors stop and wait for your answer rather than the officer's.
One visitor directly asks why you were brought there without your agreement.
You interrupt the officer and decide what will be shown.
event.family_marine_07_not_an_exhibit.te: Despite your earlier refusal, an officer is waiting with three visitors from another service. He presents your size and growth before even asking whether you want to stay.
event.family_marine_07_not_an_exhibit_i0: Speak to the visitors, not the officer
You explain directly to them what you are refusing.
Ask them to leave
You change the question: you are no longer the one expected to leave.
Accept one test you choose
You agree to show one thing only because you set the limit.
The Visitors Wait
The discomfort becomes obvious: the visitors realize they are watching something that was never negotiated with you.
Let him save face
You get to leave, but he still gets to explain why.
Correct his version in front of them
You refuse to let your consent be invented after the fact.
Ask where your father is in this decision
You bring the scene back to the family the officer claims to represent.
Saving Face
The officer tries to reframe the scene as a misunderstanding. He wants everyone to leave believing the Marine had planned for your refusal.
State what cannot happen again
You turn your refusal into an explicit rule for any future summons.
Decide not to cooperate again
You now refuse any tracking that begins without your agreement.
Only agree when you present yourself
You keep the door open only if nobody speaks about you before you do.
Your Boundary
The visitors finally leave. What remains matters more for the future: the officer now knows exactly what boundary you set and whether he respected it.
event.family_marine_07_what_marines_prot: Wait for the equipment
You stay behind the line while the trapped civilians beg everyone to hurry.
Help before the order
You get too close and part of the cart shifts dangerously.
You cannot free anyone alone and the watch commander orders you back.
You clear enough space for one civilian to breathe more easily.
You find a leverage point that lets the adults begin before all the equipment arrives.
Bring the Marines to the civilians
You pull Marines toward the trapped civilians one by one instead of waiting for the order to change.
What the Marine Protects
An overturned cart blocks a street near a Marine post. Two civilians are trapped beneath it, but the watch commander orders everyone to wait for proper equipment before moving anything.
Stay behind the line
You accept that group safety comes before the visible urgency beneath the cart.
Find a safe support
You look for a way to reduce the risk without completely ignoring the order.
Ask your father what he would do
You ask him while both the order and the trapped people are still in front of him.
It Gets Worse
A wheel cracks under the weight. By the time the equipment arrives, the cart may shift again.
Convince him to start
He sends you firmly behind the line and bans further improvisation.
He still refuses, but orders the equipment rushed in.
He authorizes a limited move using what is already secured.
He adopts your idea, assigns roles, and begins the rescue immediately.
Accept the wait
You stop pushing against the order and help prepare for the equipment.
Disobey to protect
You choose the trapped person over the exact form of the order.
Act Under Pressure
The watch commander now has to choose between maintaining the order exactly or using what you have already prepared.
Defend the procedure
You remember that protecting people also means avoiding new victims.
Defend acting quickly
You remember that an order preventing protection may need to be challenged.
Defend the safer third way
You mainly remember that obeying and disobeying were not the only two options.
After the Rescue
The civilians are finally freed. The argument continues after the emergency: did you act correctly because everyone is safe, or despite the way you acted?
event.family_marine_07_fallback_home_dut: You start by protecting the house.
You start with what will be hardest to replace.
You start with what is directly waiting for your father.
Your father leaves three things to do before he returns: close the shutters, fetch water, and keep the meal warm. Only one can be done immediately.
You show him you did not forget the other tasks, only chose which one could least afford to wait.
You simply finish the list instead of seeking his approval.
Give one task back to him
You remind him that holding the household together has not become only your job.
Your father returns earlier than expected and immediately sees the order in which you chose to hold the household together.
event.family_marine_07_fallback_service_: Follow the protocol exactly
You repeat the gestures you were shown.
Ask what it is for
You interrupt the ritual before reproducing it.
Add a personal note
You slip something personal into a service formality.
Service as Inheritance
Each year your household must hand a small service record or insignia to the local office. This time, the adult asks you to make the handoff yourself.
Accept the ritual
You understand the gesture exists precisely because it repeats.
Say what it means to you
You refuse to let the office decide alone what the gesture means.
Make the handoff and nothing more
You complete the formality without giving it more weight.
Why We Do It
The clerk explains that the handoff serves both the archives and as a reminder of which families remain tied to service.
Keep it as a Marine tradition
You accept that the institution is part of how your family tells its story.
Keep it as a family tradition
You reclaim the ritual for the household rather than the office.
Treat it as routine
You learn to move through the institution without giving meaning to every gesture.
The Gesture That Remains
The clerk files the document. The ritual is over, but you chose whether it belonged mostly to the Marine, your family, or simply the calendar.
event.family_marine_07_fallback_belongin: Say exactly what you need
You give a solution before anyone offers a bad one.
Try their first idea
You agree to test their first idea before judging it.
Adapt on your own
You begin moving the equipment without waiting.
Finding Your Place
A base activity once again needs adjusting for your body. This time, the adults look directly at you instead of trying to guess what you need.
Fix it with them
You explain the new problem before it becomes a new habit.
Make do
You accept an imperfect solution so the activity can continue.
Start over differently
You refuse to let a half-working adaptation become the standard.
An Imperfect Solution
The first adaptation works halfway. It solves one problem and creates another.
Remember it can be fixed together
You keep the idea that an institution can learn if someone clearly says what does not work.
Remember you can make do
You learn to move forward even when the system only adapts halfway.
Keep your own method
You trust what you build yourself more than solutions designed for you.
Your Way of Doing It
When the activity finally begins, nobody can pretend the solution appeared on its own.
event.family_marine_10_report_against_hi: Say you believe him
You take his side before knowing the details of the accusation.
Read the report anyway
You catch one sentence out of context and immediately read it against him.
The jargon leaves you with more suspicion than answers.
You understand the delay let civilians leave the area before the intervention.
You notice the report omits the civilians from its main summary.
Ask what he did
You refuse to choose between trust and accusation without hearing him speak.
The Report Against Him
An official summons reaches the household: your father is accused of delaying an order during an operation, allowing a target to escape. He asks you not to read the report.
Believe his reason
You separate the act he is accused of from the reason he gives.
Ask who can confirm it
You ask him for a witness, not a better story.
Say he still disobeyed
You refuse to let good intentions erase the chain of command.
What They Blame Him For
The report is true about one thing: your father did delay the order. He says he waited for three families to clear the quay before letting the patrol move in.
Support his choice, not his method
You refuse to turn the case into total innocence or guilt.
Defend his refusal fully
For you, the result justifies the risk he took against the order.
Say he should have reported it
You recognize the civilians were protected but reject him deciding the rule alone.
Another Version
A Marine collecting the summons confirms the civilians, but adds that your father could have warned his superior instead of acting alone.
Say you support him without absolving him
You keep the family bond without automatically declaring him right.
Say you stand with him
You choose loyalty to him when the institution is testing it.
Say you need to think
You refuse to produce a family answer just because a hearing demands one.
What You Owe Him
Before leaving for the hearing, your father asks only one thing: do not let his uniform decide for you what you think of him.
event.family_marine_10_they_discuss_your: Ask what they have planned
You enter the conversation instead of letting it define you from outside.
Interrupt them
Your interruption is treated as childish impatience and the conversation resumes over your head.
They listen for a second, then turn back to your father.
Both officers stop speaking about you in the third person.
One closes the file and asks you directly what you want to know.
Ask what happens if you say no
The room goes quiet before an adult finds an answer.
They Already Discuss Your Uniform
Two officers discuss a future recruitment file, your aptitude, and where “a child from this family” might begin. Nobody has asked whether you want to serve.
Ask for the conditions
You want to know what the favor expects in return.
Accept being watched
You accept the attention without yet promising the uniform.
Reject the plan
You refuse to let the file advance before your decision.
The Offer Before the Age
They speak of observation, recommendations, and an easier entry once Active begins. It is a promise, but also an expectation.
Let him sign
You let him commit the family to this preparation.
Take the pen from him
You remind everyone the file carries your name, not his.
Ask what he really wants
You force your father to separate his pride from your future.
What Your Father Does With It
Your father receives the pen meant for family authorization. The officers wait for him to speak before you.
Say you want to see where it leads
You accept the inheritance as a serious possibility, not yet an obligation.
Say it will be on your terms
You reject a prewritten future while keeping the Marine among your choices.
Say nobody will choose for you
You close the file without necessarily closing the door on the Marine itself.
Your Future Is Not Signed
The file remains open on the table. What matters now is not the paper, but how you accept or reject the expectation placed on you.
event.family_marine_10_argument_through_: Listen to the end
You stay close enough to hear what they avoided saying in front of you.
Enter the room
You refuse to let the argument continue as if it did not concern you.
Leave the house
You refuse to become the third argument in their fight.

Your parents argue behind a partition. Your mother discovered your father accepted a more dangerous assignment without telling her. The word “family” comes up more often than “Marine.”
Say your mother is right about the decision
You separate the job from how your father treated the household.
Say the posting may matter
You acknowledge his work may have reasons beyond the household.
Say they should have decided together
You refuse to turn duty and family into permanent sides.

Say you want him to stay
You answer the question even if it perhaps should never have been put to you.
Say you want to understand his mission
You refuse to ask only for comfort without understanding the work at stake.
Refuse to choose between them
You hand back the decision they had just placed on you.
“And You?”
The argument stops when one parent asks what you want. The other immediately says it is not your job to settle their problem.
Stay with your mother
Your mother becomes a real counterweight to the idea that service always decides first.
Stay with your father
You accept more of service's cost without erasing what it does to the household.
Ask them to decide together
You refuse to let their conflict become your permanent side.
After the Argument
The posting is not yet settled, but the question of how the family should decide together is clearer.
event.family_marine_10_keep_this_quiet.c: You first agree to protect what he told you.
You refuse to call it a secret without knowing who it protects.
You tell him his trust cannot decide what is true for everyone else.
event.family_marine_10_keep_this_quiet.t: After the stall incident, your father learns an internal report minimizes the vendor's losses. He asks you not to repeat what he admitted to you that evening.
event.family_marine_10_keep_this_quiet_i: Protect your father
You accept that truth can also hurt someone you love.
Think first of the vendor
You refuse to forget the person already paying the price of silence.
Look for a truth that does not accuse everyone
You look for what can be said without inventing or revealing everything.
Why Stay Quiet
Your father explains an inquiry could punish him and fall on the whole patrol. He does not say the report is fair; he says speaking will have a price.
Tell everything
You mix what you saw with what your father told you, weakening your account.
The investigator writes it down but repeatedly asks whether you are sure.
You clearly separate what you saw from what your father told you.
Your account forces the investigator to reopen the report section minimizing the losses.
Say only what you saw
You protect the confidence without lying about the lost crates.
Refuse to answer
You keep the secret at the cost of a question now visible in the file.
The Chance to Speak
The next day, an investigator simply asks whether you saw the losses at the stall. Your father is not in the room.
Say you kept his confidence
You protect your father, but you know exactly what that protection leaves out of the report.
Say you did not lie
You refuse to choose between betraying a confidence and denying what you saw.
Say truth came before him
You accept that your relationship pays part of the price for what you said.
What Silence Protects
When you return, your father asks what you said. For the first time, the secret is also a decision between you.
event.family_marine_10_tell_us_what_mari: Read the official text
You take the sheet and follow the prepared words exactly.
Speak in your own words
You stumble under the attention and one awkward phrase becomes what everyone remembers.
Your message comes out less clearly than in your head, but it is yours.
You tell a concrete experience instead of reciting a slogan.
The room stops looking at the official sheet and actually listens to you.
Give the microphone back
You refuse to be used as a ready-made answer to a question about your own life.
Tell Us What Marine Means
At a family ceremony, the organizer hands you the small microphone: “Tell us what it means to grow up in a Marine family.” The official text lies in front of you.
Repeat your point more clearly
You refuse to let a confused reaction replace what you meant.
Let the host conclude
You let the host return the ceremony to its planned frame.
Speak to the other children
You shift the conversation toward those who actually live what is being discussed.
The Room Reacts
Families, officers, and other children do not react the same way. The organizer tries to regain control of the moment.
Say the Marine must change
You state that the institution itself is part of the question.
Say your family is the subject
You refuse to turn every family difficulty into a political manifesto.
Say you were speaking about yourself
You refuse to stretch your words beyond what you lived.
What an Adult Hears
After the ceremony, a Marine stops you. He wants to know whether your words criticized the Marine itself or only how some families are treated.
Keep the ideal of protection
You separate what the Marine claims to protect from all the imperfect ways it does so.
Keep your own words
You decide nobody will define your inheritance for you.
Keep distance from the symbol
You accept your family without having to love how the institution stages it.
Your Own Definition
The microphone is put away, but the sentence you keep for yourself matters more than the one that will remain in the report.
You place your fingers on the letters as if checking they are real.
You refuse to let the plaque be the only available version.
You refuse to give the plaque the power to impose a memory on you.
Your father's name appears on a base plaque. Beneath it, one clean sentence summarizes his whole career. The old sergeant stops beside you without comment.
event.family_marine_10_his_name_on_wall_: Accept that plaques simplify
You accept that a wall is not a complete story.
Tell the sergeant what you remember
You rebuild aloud the less polished version you chose to keep.
Ask whether the wording can change
You ask whether official memory can still be corrected.
The Chosen Words
The plaque speaks of duty and courage. It says nothing about the broken bridge, the mistake, or what he had to repair.
Keep both versions
You let the plaque exist without giving it the final word.
Prefer the private memory
You choose the imperfect story nobody engraved.
Prefer the plaque
You choose the version that gives his service a clear, shareable shape.
Memory Does Not Belong to the Wall
The old sergeant tells you the plaque belongs to the base. What you say about your father belongs only to those who knew him.
Keep his complexity
You refuse to believe loving his memory requires simplifying it.
Keep his service
You choose to make his service a central part of what he left you.
Keep your name separate from his
You refuse to let his inscription automatically become your inheritance.
What Remains Yours
When you leave the wall, the name stays behind. The way you carry it leaves with you.
event.family_marine_10_giant_offer_too_e: Agree to hear it
You accept the meeting without accepting the program yet.
Ask for the terms first
The officer treats your request as needless suspicion and presents the program without answering precisely.
You get vague promises, not written limits.
The officer has to specify who can summon you, how often, and for what.
He agrees to write down your conditions before presenting his own.
Refuse the file
You refuse to let a program already exist around you without your agreement.
An Offer Too Early
An officer arrives with a file prepared for you: regular training, quarterly measurements, and access to Marine equipment. You are only ten, but the program already talks about your future.
Focus on training
You separate what can genuinely teach you something from the rest of the program.
Point at the demonstrations
You ask why your learning must be shown to people who do not train you.
Point at the tracking
You ask when the program stops measuring and starts actually teaching you.
The Program
The file provides for tests, growth tracking, and occasional demonstrations before senior staff. It promises adapted equipment and privileged access to instructors.
Say strength is for protection
You bring the program back to what you did during the previous demonstration.
Say you are not a weapon
You reject language that talks about your body before it talks about you.
Accept being evaluated
You accept that your potential interests the Marine as long as participation remains your choice.
What They Want From You
The officer finally uses the words “strategic potential.” He says the Marine wants to know what a Giant trained early might contribute later.
Make them write your limits
The officer rewrites your limits as optional recommendations.
He accepts some limits but refuses to make them binding.
He writes that demonstrations require your agreement and that training takes priority over spectacle.
He signs the limits himself and has the document countersigned before returning it to you.
Refuse unless it is written
You refuse to let verbal promises commit years of your life.
Accept without adding clauses
You accept the program as offered.
Your Conditions
You now have the file, the pen, and the officer's attention. If the program continues, this is where your limits can become written.
Keep a signed copy
Your limits now exist in the same administrative language as their expectations.
Refuse further tracking
You leave the program rather than accept limits the Marine can ignore.
Accept the program as written
You choose access and training despite what the file expects from your body.
What Stays in the File

You let the presentation unfold as the officers prepared it.
Your interruption is drowned by applause and the official immediately takes the microphone back.
You speak, but the official immediately summarizes your words his way.
The visitors stop looking at the official and look at you.
You completely reverse the presentation: questions now come directly to you.
Leave the center of the yard
You refuse to be living proof of a sentence nobody asked you to approve.
During an official visit, a senior Marine places you at the center of a yard and presents you as “proof the Marine knows how to make room for everyone.” You recognize the staging before he finishes.
event.family_marine_10_giant_on_display_: Show only what you chose
You limit the demonstration to what you had previously agreed to.
Explain how you got your limits
You make visible that this place was never offered without conflict.
Say you represent only yourself
You refuse to be used as general proof about all Giants or all families.
What the Crowd Sees
The visitors watch you as much as the uniform around you. The scene can still serve the official staging, or become something else.
Let him conclude
You get peace at the price of letting him narrate your opposition his way.
Correct him in front of the visitors
You refuse to let your consent be invented after the fact.
Ask the crowd what they heard
You take away the official's monopoly on the conclusion.
Saving the Presentation
The official tries to conclude that your freedom to speak proves the system works. He turns your refusal into an argument for himself.
Keep the last word
You turn the display into a statement nobody had planned.
Accept being a symbol
You accept your image serving an institution you still believe can keep its promise.
Decide this was the last time
You close the door on any further staging of your body.
Your Voice or Their Symbol
As the yard empties, you know whether the visitors will leave with your story or only the image the Marine wanted to display.
event.family_marine_10_protect_or_obey.c: You follow the order, hoping someone will reach the injured civilian another way.
The gate nearly tears your hands away and jams halfway in a dangerous position.
You cannot hold it alone and a Marine forces you to let go.
You gain enough time for the injured civilian to reach the opening.
You hold the gate until a Marine finally helps you instead of closing it.
You refuse to choose immediately between the gate and the person.
event.family_marine_10_protect_or_obey.t: A fire breaks out near a dock warehouse. The order is to close the gate to contain the crowd, but an injured civilian is still on the other side as the lock begins to drop.
event.family_marine_10_protect_or_obey_i: Hold the line
You help prevent the crowd from turning the fire into a larger disaster.
Go through to help the injured person
You make the trapped person your immediate priority.
Use a rope over the barrier
You look for a solution that does not reopen the gate to the whole crowd.
The Gate Comes Down
The smoke thickens. The watch commander repeats the order because the crowd is already pressing from the other side of the dock.
Disobey and continue
You get trapped too and two Marines have to come get both of you.
You help poorly and complicate the maneuver before the Marines regain control.
You reach the injured civilian and bring them to the safe passage.
You protect the injured civilian while guiding others toward an exit that does not reopen the crowd.
Return behind the gate
You obey the final order and leave the rescue to the adults.
Force a third solution
Your idea comes too late and briefly distracts the adults from the useful maneuver.
The idea does not work fast enough; the commander refuses to change the plan.
You find a route that preserves the closure while reaching the injured civilian.
Your solution becomes the post's new plan for the rest of the fire.

The injured civilian slips to the ground. The watch commander sees you act and gives one final clear order: “Get back behind the gate.”
Say the order was protecting people too
You refuse to caricature the order simply because it had a visible cost.
Say an order is not enough
You state that a rule must still be judged by what it actually protects.
Say another solution was needed
You reject the idea that the only options were obedience or opening everything.

Keep discipline as a safeguard
You accept that protection without a framework can become another danger.
Keep protection before obedience
You decide an order loses legitimacy when it demands abandoning someone who can still be saved.
Keep the third way
You refuse to let authority make you forget that a situation can be changed rather than merely endured.
What You Call Duty

event.family_marine_10_fallback_duty.cho: You protect the house at the expense of the rest.
You prioritize evenings when someone still needs to work or read.
You prioritize what lets your father continue serving.
event.family_marine_10_fallback_duty.tex: A pay deduction arrives after one of your father's missions. This month the household must choose between repairing a leak, buying more lamp oil, or replacing worn boots.
event.family_marine_10_fallback_duty_i01: You accept that holding a household together sometimes means choosing which problem waits.
Ask your father what he would sacrifice
You refuse to let his work create a shortage he alone does not have to face.
You look for how to reduce several problems instead of solving one perfectly.
The first purchase solves one problem and makes the other two more visible. The household can no longer pretend service's cost exists only on paper.
event.family_marine_10_fallback_duty_i02: You refuse to let every family shortage be automatically absorbed in the name of service.
Accept that service has a price
You accept more fully that the household also pays for what it believes matters.
Ask him to make it up another way
You reject the choice between total support and rejection: duty must also give something back to the household.

event.family_marine_10_fallback_family.c: You step forward when the clerk opens the way.
You stay in the line where you arrived.
Ask whether your neighbor can pass too
You turn the personal privilege into a question for the clerk.
event.family_marine_10_fallback_family.t: In a base queue, a clerk recognizes your family name and offers to move you ahead “for services rendered.” The other families hear perfectly.
event.family_marine_10_fallback_family_i: You refuse to pretend the advantage does not exist.
Say you did not earn it
You clearly separate family history from your personal merit.
Use the access to help someone
You look for a way to turn the advantage into something that does not stop with you.
Whether you move ahead or not, everyone now knows your name can open a door faster than theirs.
You accept the inheritance but attach an obligation toward others to it.
You refuse to let your father's service become your automatic shortcut.
Use the system without idealizing it
You learn that knowing rules and access does not require confusing them with justice.

The line finally moves. The privilege is no longer hypothetical: you decided what to do when the family name acts before you.
event.family_marine_10_fallback_identity: Carry the sign
You accept the role prepared for you.
Ask to change how it is done
You accept the ceremony, not necessarily the exact place assigned to you.
Refuse to represent the group
You refuse to let one person serve as a summary of every family present.

You give the role your own meaning before the clerk does it for you.
Offer to share the role
You refuse to let representation rest on one person.
Return the sign before departure
You change your mind before the procession turns your presence into a symbol.

Say you represent your family
You accept the family inheritance without pretending to speak for the whole Marine.
Say you represent only yourself
You refuse to let family affiliation turn your identity into a public function.
Accept carrying the symbol
You accept the Marine as part of what you want to show the world.

You close your fingers around it without answering yet.
You keep your hand open and ask why the insignia has come to you today.
You refuse to let an object turn hesitation into commitment.

event.family_marine_13_insignia_in_palm_: Ask what he did with it

Look at what it cost the household

You keep the insignia as an inheritance you choose to continue in your own way.
Keep the insignia, not the career
You keep the family story without making it your first profession.
You refuse to let uncertainty at thirteen become a career promise.

event.family_marine_13_your_future_is_yo: Finally exhale

Ask why it took so long
You refuse to pretend the years of expectation never weighed on you.
Ask whether the Marine is still possible
You want to know whether freedom includes the right to choose the inheritance.

You look for what is still worth keeping in the idea of protection.
Ask what to avoid
You turn family history into warnings as much as inheritance.
Say you want to decide alone
You finally take the decision out of the adults' hands.

You keep the Marine as a future possibility, but not as your starting point.

event.family_marine_13_chest_he_left.cho: You ask for a few minutes before anyone reads over your shoulder.
You refuse to let the inheritance become a solitary conversation.

You prefer hearing the first sentence in another voice.
event.family_marine_13_chest_he_left.tex: A chest from your father is finally opened before you. Among his service belongings, a journal and a letter bear your name, written long before anyone knew which career you would choose.
event.family_marine_13_chest_he_left_i01: You start with everything he probably would never have put on a plaque.
You follow people rather than ranks through his story.
You look for what he believed at the end rather than what he believed at the beginning.

event.family_marine_13_chest_he_left_i02: Read it as an invitation to continue
You hear a reason to try wearing the uniform differently.
You refuse to turn a family letter into a posthumous order.
You mainly keep what he wanted to stop you from repeating.

event.family_marine_13_chest_he_left_i03: You choose the Marine without erasing the pages showing how it can go wrong.
Keep his memory without following his career
You keep his whole story, but your first profession will be your own.
Refuse to let a letter decide
You take the journal as inheritance and refuse to let it become an instruction.

event.family_marine_13_wear_it_better.ch: You refuse a vague confession when it becomes inheritance.
You refuse to let his mistakes become his whole career.
You look for the reason that survived his own criticism.
event.family_marine_13_wear_it_better.ti: Wear It Better Than I Did

event.family_marine_13_wear_it_better_i0: Keep both

Keep the family cost

Take only the insignia

Give both back

You choose to begin as a Marine recruit, using his mistakes as warnings rather than excuses.
Keep the insignia without enlisting
You accept his family inheritance without making his profession your starting point.
Refuse both
You refuse to let his wish for you to do better become another expectation placed on you.

event.family_marine_13_duty_not_obedienc: Open the report

Ask what you should do with it

You know what you reject, but not yet how you would apply it day to day.
You clearly distinguish discipline, responsibility, and blind obedience.

Keep your conclusion private
You refuse to turn your inheritance into a public declaration before Active even begins.
Ask whether the Marine truly accepts that position

Protect outside the uniform

Keep the question open

event.family_marine_13_our_name_is_not_t: Help return the symbols

You make sure the family's version does not disappear with the official material.
Ask whether they want your name too
You make explicit the difference between leaving an institution and erasing an origin.

Say you have not rejected the idea of the Marine
You refuse to let the family break be interpreted as your final opinion.
Say your name remains yours
You refuse to let the institution turn separation into family shame.

Remove your name
You choose to make the family break apply to your own Active start as well.
Keep your name on the list

Say you will decide without their list
You reject both automatic enrollment and automatic rejection.

Begin Active outside the Marine
You turn the family break into a real professional separation when Active begins.
Join the Marine anyway
You reject how they treated your family, not the idea that you might wear the uniform differently.
Begin civilian without closing the door
You refuse to turn the break into a permanent professional identity.
Your Name, Your Decision

event.family_marine_13_what_remains_of_h: Read the service pages first
You begin with the missions and choices he made in uniform.
Read the personal pages first
You begin with what he wrote when nobody asked him to represent the Marine.
Mix the pages
You refuse to artificially separate the man from the Marine before reading him.
What Remains of Him
After the plaque, the old sergeant brings you the last pages of your father's personal journal. “The wall keeps his name. This is what was left in his locker.”
Keep his service ideal
You refuse to let his contradictions erase the people he wanted to protect.
Keep the father first
You refuse to make rank the center of your memory.
Keep both without reconciling them
You accept that a memory can remain contradictory without becoming false.

Some pages speak of duty, others of home. Several show your father himself did not always know where one ended and the other began.
Take the journal
You take the object containing his contradictions rather than one that summarizes them.
Copy only a few pages
You decide which parts of his story should actually travel with you.
Keep it all closed
You keep the journal without promising to reread it immediately.
One Object to Keep
Among his belongings, you choose the journal rather than an official symbol. It is the object that will stay with you after the ceremonies end.
Serve in his memory
You choose the Marine without pretending that choice completes or repairs your father's life.
Keep the father, not the profession
You keep his journal as inheritance and leave his uniform in his story.
Choose your own first path
You enter Active without asking his memory to choose your profession.
His Profession Is Not Your Answer

event.family_marine_13_decide_for_yourse: Ask for advice, not a decision
You still accept adult experience without returning your choice to them.
Say you already know
You refuse to drag out a decision you have built for years.
Say you will not decide today
You treat delay as a legitimate decision too.
Decide for Yourself
After years of adults speaking about your name, body, or duty, the person beside you finally pushes all the forms away: “This answer has to come from you.”
Think about whom you want to protect
You turn inheritance into a concrete question rather than a symbol.
Think about what you refuse to surrender
You judge each option by what it demands from your autonomy.
Think about the price you accept
